analysis.one_liner: Restores federal pre-approval for voting rule changes in states with recent voting rights violations.
analysis.headline: The Senate blocked the bill from ever reaching the floor when a procedural vote failed 50-49, short of the 60 needed, with all but one Republican voting no.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have re-established the Voting Rights Act's "preclearance" system, under which states and localities with recent records of voting rights violations must get Justice Department or court approval before changing their election rules. It set a new formula: any state with 15 or more voting rights violations over 25 years (or 10 or more, at least one by the state itself) would need pre-approval for a decade, and it spelled out specific changes—like new ID requirements, fewer polling places, or redistricting—that would always require review. It also added public notice rules for voting changes, expanded voting access on tribal lands, and increased criminal penalties for interfering with election workers and polling places.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters—especially Black, Hispanic, Asian American, Native, and language-minority voters—in states and counties with documented histories of voting discrimination, who would gain an upfront federal check on changes to their election rules instead of having to sue after the fact.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters in jurisdictions with voting-rights violation records

how_it_helps.text: Restores preclearance with a new formula: states with 15 or more voting rights violations in 25 years, or 10 or more with at least one by the state itself, need federal pre-approval for voting changes for 10 years; counties and other subdivisions with 3 or more violations are covered separately.

Lists specific 'covered practices' that always require pre-approval, such as new or stricter voter ID or proof-of-citizenship requirements, changes to at-large elections and redistricting, reducing voting locations or hours, and cutting multilingual voting materials.
Requires states and localities to publicly announce changes to voting rules and polling place resources within 48 hours, so voters can see what changed before an election.
Expands voting access on tribal lands and adds protections for election workers, polling places, and election infrastructure, including stiffer criminal penalties for threats and damage.
Lets the Justice Department require states to produce documents and answer questions when enforcing voting rights laws, and clarifies that individual voters as well as the Attorney General can sue.

analysis.who_pays: State legislatures and local election officials in covered jurisdictions, who would face a federal review process (up to 60 days, or a three-judge court) before implementing election rule changes, plus the administrative cost of notice and documentation requirements.

drawbacks.text: Covered states and counties would bear real administrative costs: pre-clearance review or litigation before implementing any covered practice, public notice of voting changes and polling resources within 48 hours, and responses to Justice Department information demands.

Changes made within 30 days of an election would face a lower bar for court intervention, and courts would weigh the public's interest in expanding ballot access heavily, which opponents of federal election oversight view as tilting election litigation toward challengers.

The formula keys off past court judgments and Justice Department objections over a 25-year lookback, meaning jurisdictions are judged by history rather than current conduct—a design critics say is outdated and one-sided, though the bill allows jurisdictions to 'bail out' with a court declaratory judgment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voters in covered jurisdictions the upside is substantial: discrimination claims could be stopped before an election rather than litigated afterward, and specific rollback practices—fewer polling places, stricter ID, removed multilingual materials—would face review by default. The cost falls on election administrators, who would absorb review timelines and paperwork, and on any jurisdiction that wants to change election rules quickly. The bill includes escape valves (bailout, expedited review for emergencies, grants to small jurisdictions) but the review burden is real. The bill never got past a procedural vote, so the tradeoff was never tested in practice.

outcome.mechanism: A motion to cut off debate so the Senate could even begin considering the bill failed 50-49 on November 3, 2021—short of the 60 votes needed—so the bill never got an up-or-down vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Leahy introduced the bill on October 5, 2021, with 46 of 48 Senate Democrats and both independents as cosponsors, and it was placed directly on the Senate calendar.
On November 1, 2021, Majority Leader Schumer made a motion to proceed to the bill and immediately filed a cloture motion—the step needed to end debate and move forward.
On November 3, 2021, cloture failed 50-49: 47 of 48 Democrats and both independents voted yes, but only 1 of 50 Republicans did, far short of the 60 required.
Because the vote was only on whether to begin consideration, the bill never received a vote on its substance, and it expired with the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State legislatures and election officials who would have been subject to federal preclearance remain free to change election rules without pre-approval, and the Senate Republicans who blocked consideration avoided a floor debate on federal oversight of state election laws.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State officials who would have faced preclearance

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act and recruited 46 Democratic and both independent senators as cosponsors.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Made the motion to bring the bill up for consideration and filed the cloture motion to end debate on moving forward.

for.name: 47 of 48 Senate Democrats plus both independents
for.role: Democratic caucus and independents voting to proceed
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on cloture to allow the bill to be considered (Manchin was the lone Democrat voting no).

for.name: Bernie Sanders and Angus King
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and voted yes on cloture.

against.name: 48 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on cloture, denying the 60 votes needed to begin consideration of the bill.

against.name: Joe Manchin
against.what_they_did: The only Democrat to vote no on cloture, joining Republicans in blocking consideration.

against.name: Lisa Murkowski
against.what_they_did: The only Republican to vote yes on cloture, siding with Democrats to allow consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost entirely by party: 47 of 48 Democrats and 2 of 2 independents voted yes, while 48 of 50 Republicans voted no, leaving the bill 10 votes short of the 60 needed.

industries.industry: State legislatures and election officials in jurisdictions with voting rights violation records
industries.note: The bill would have required them to obtain federal pre-approval for most changes to election rules and to publish detailed public notices, replacing discretion with federal review. Its defeat leaves their authority over election changes unreviewed unless voters sue after the fact.

industries.industry: Voting rights litigation bar and civil rights organizations
industries.note: The bill expanded who can sue, clarified attorneys' fees, and created presumptions favoring relief near elections, strengthening the toolkit of groups and lawyers who challenge discriminatory voting practices. With the bill dead, those challenges remain harder and slower.
